idiom_name: scala.collection.immutable persistent collections + case class copy()
implementation_notes: Copy-on-write is the default mode of the standard library: scala.collection.immutable is imported by default, its collections are persistent, and an update returns a new collection that shares most of its structure with the old one - the documentation states that persistent collections and side-effect-free operations mean you need not worry about accidentally corrupting existing collections, and that interference between iterators and collection updates is eliminated. Case classes give the value-level form through copy(): the compiler generates a method that returns a new instance with the named fields replaced while unchanged fields are shared. The refcounted handle/body structure is not needed - the immutable collection and the case class replace it - and val plus immutable-by-default stops accidental mutation at compile time.
code_sketch:
case class Settings(host: String, port: Int = 8080, tags: Vector[String] = Vector.empty)

val base = Settings(host = "db", tags = Vector("prod"))
val moved = base.copy(port = 5432)        // new value, base untouched
val extended = base.tags :+ "eu-west"     // shares structure with base.tags
pitfalls: Nested mutable state defeats it: a case class holding an Array or a mutable.Map shares that reference, so copy() yields a new outer object with the same mutable innards.
Persistent updates are O(log n) path copies, so repeated single-element updates in a tight loop belong in a builder or a bulk operation.

A mutable collection is one import away (scala.collection.mutable.ListBuffer), and even immutable values are unsafe to publish without synchronization when other threads may observe them mid-construction.
Equality is structural, so two different versions can be ==; use reference equality only where snapshot identity really matters.
